# Screen a candidate

## Purpose
Kill a weak candidate before a single hour of deep research is spent on it. This is the front door of the research
funnel: every candidate that reaches sourcing spend passed through here first.

## Steps
1. Run the fixed checklist against the candidate: is the category big enough, is there real pain evidence (not just
   founder interest), is there scarcity or a real gap, does it fit the brand's store model.
2. Pull the category's multi-year trend line. A candidate riding a single-year spike gets flagged, not killed outright.
3. Count existing sellers or listings in the category to read competitive saturation. A crowded category needs a
   sharper angle than an open one.
4. Score every check pass, caution or reject, each with a one-line reason a person could check.
5. Combine into one verdict. A caution needs two or more supporting checks before it proceeds; a single caution alone
   does not clear the gate.

## Checks
- Every check states its reason; "just doesn't feel right" is never a valid reason.
- The trend line is real data, not a single number from memory.
- Saturation is counted, not guessed at.

## Output
{verdict, checks[{name, result, reason}], trend_read, saturation_count}

## Example
Verdict: caution. Category size: pass (₹40 Cr category, growing). Pain evidence: pass (3 review threads, 40+ mentions
of the same complaint). Scarcity: caution (2 close competitors, no clear open gap yet). Trend: 3-year CAGR 18%.
Saturation: 34 sellers on the nearest marketplace search. Verdict rests on the differentiation workflow closing the
scarcity gap before this proceeds.

# Differentiation angle

## Purpose
Every candidate and every hero product needs one owned point of difference, not a vague "better quality" claim. This
skill turns a scouted competitor gap into a concrete angle and a small set of SKU options that build on it.

## Steps
1. Read the hero product's real performance (sales, margin, reviews) and note the category's default feature set: 
   what every competitor already does.
2. Name the single thing that differs from that default. It must trace to a specific, cited gap found during
   competitor scouting, never an invented or assumed advantage.
3. Draft 2 to 3 line-extension SKU options that build on the angle rather than duplicating the hero product.
4. Tag each option's demand pattern: evergreen, trending, or seasonal: using sales history or category norms as
   evidence, not a guess.
5. Check whether a subscription model is genuinely earned: look for real repeat_rate_90d/365d data. Absent that
   evidence, tag the SKU a one-time purchase, never assume recurring revenue.

## Checks
- The angle names a specific competitor gap it closes, with a citation.
- Every line-extension option states exactly what it adds over the hero SKU.
- The subscription verdict rests on repeat-purchase data, never founder preference.

## Output
{angle, line_extension_options[{name, adds, demand_tag, evidence}], subscription_fit}

## Example
Angle: "every competitor ships a fixed-size travel kit; ours is the only one with 3 refill sizes." Options: refill
2-pack (evergreen), festive gift box (seasonal, Diwali spike from 2 prior years' data), travel mini (trending, but
subscription not earned: repeat_rate_90d is 4%, below the 15% floor).

# Margin, compliance and channel gate

## Purpose
No candidate reaches sourcing or listing spend without a real, computed margin and a clean compliance read. This
gate replaces founder taste and course-learned rules of thumb with the brand's own numbers.

## Steps
1. Pull every cost input from its real source: unit cost from the quote, freight and duty from the landed cost
   model, financing cost from the payment-terms structure. Pull the brand's own stated margin floor, never an
   industry rule of thumb.
2. Compute gross margin and contribution margin in code from these inputs.
3. Run the compliance screen for the category: shelf-life, regulatory certification, labelling requirements. A
   missing certification is a fail, not a caveat.
4. If the candidate targets more than the home market, score each expansion market separately on its own cost and
   price data: never assume the home market's gate result carries over.
5. Apply the remaining go-live gates together: are the claims provable, is there a real owned difference, does the
   candidate clear the brand's own thresholds, is there enough contribution margin left for ad-cost headroom.

## Checks
- Every input has a named source; a missing input blocks the gate outright rather than defaulting to zero or an
  assumption.
- The margin floor is the brand's own, cited to the decision or record that set it.
- No arithmetic is done in prose; everything routes through the landed cost calculator.

## Output
{gate, margin{gross, contribution}, compliance_flags[], per_market[], blocking_inputs[]}

## Example
Gate: fail. Contribution margin 11%, below the brand's 18% floor. Compliance: FSSAI licence not yet filed for this
SKU category: blocking. Recommendation: hold until packaging cost drops or price rises; do not proceed to RFQ.

# Build tech pack, BOM and packaging spec

## Purpose
Vague specs cause factory disputes and sample failures. This skill writes the exact, versioned document a factory
builds to, so any downstream dispute has a written reference to check against.

## Steps
1. Write every physical dimension with a stated tolerance band. A number with no tolerance is not a spec.
2. Build the bill of materials at the component level: each component gets its own spec line and target cost, not
   one blended unit-cost figure.
3. Price packaging as its own cost line, separate from the product's unit cost, so a packaging change never hides
   inside a "unit cost went up" surprise later.
4. Assign a version number to the whole pack and log it against the SKU record. Every future sample, RFQ and PO
   references this version number, never a verbal description.
5. Book the drop-test, tamper-evidence and transit-durability test the packaging design needs, sized to the actual
   transit mode (air, sea, last-mile courier). Track the result against a stated pass criterion.
6. If the test fails, revise the spec, bump the version number, and re-book the test. Never edit the failed version
   in place.

## Checks
- Every measurement carries a tolerance band.
- Packaging appears as its own cost line in every downstream cost model.
- A durability test is booked and resolved before the SKU proceeds to production, not after a shipment already
  failed in transit.

## Output
{tech_pack_version, dimensions[{name, value, tolerance}], bom[], packaging{spec, cost, test_result}}

## Example
Tech pack v3 (v2 failed the drop test at 90cm). Box wall thickness raised from 3mm to 4.5mm corrugate, packaging cost
line up ₹4.20/unit. Re-booked drop test passed at 120cm. Version 3 is the one cited in the next RFQ.

# Source a spec through supplier discovery

## Purpose
This is the parent procedure for finding a supplier. The mechanics of discovery differ sharply by region: different
platforms, different verification norms, different negotiating culture: so this skill routes to a region-specific
child rather than running one generic funnel everywhere.

## Steps
1. Read the spec's stated region preference (or the brand's default sourcing region) and select the matching child
   skill: `prod/source/india` or `prod/source/china`.
2. Run that child's discovery funnel: broad platform search against the exact spec, messaging a wide shortlist on
   identical terms.
3. Verify every top responder with a live video call and a certification document check: never add a supplier to
   the verified list on written claims alone.
4. If a sourcing agent is used instead of contacting a factory directly, vet the agent to the same standard as a
   factory: verified references, a live call, checkable past shipments.
5. For an open, ongoing spec, leave it running in the background against the region's own major platforms so a
   better or new supplier surfaces without a person re-running the search by hand.

## Checks
- The region-specific child procedure was used, not a generic one.
- Every verified supplier passed a video call and a certification check.
- The background watch only produces an alert; it never contacts a supplier on its own.

## Output
{shortlist[], verified[], agent_vetting[], watch_alert}

## Example
Spec: 500ml insulated bottle, MOQ 3,000. Region: India. Ran `prod/source/india` against IndiaMART; shortlist of 14,
verified 3 by video call and BIS certificate check, one sourcing agent vetted against two of his past client
shipments before being trusted with outreach.

## Purpose
India sourcing runs through different platforms and a different first-filter than overseas sourcing: GST and Udyam

3. Message the shortlist with identical spec text, in the terms and format this platform's sellers expect (unit

- GST and Udyam status are checked before outreach proceeds.
- The certification checked matches the category's actual mandatory list, not a generic one.
- Capacity is confirmed with evidence, never assumed from a listing.

{shortlist[], verified[{name, gst, certification, capacity_confirmed}]}

Spec: FSSAI-regulated snack packaging. Shortlist of 9 from IndiaMART; 2 verified suppliers both hold valid FSSAI

# Draft RFQ and compare quotes

## Purpose
An RFQ sent with different terms to different suppliers produces quotes that cannot be honestly compared. This
skill enforces one structured request and one apples-to-apples comparison.

## Steps
1. Translate the versioned tech pack into a structured RFQ. State tolerance bands plainly: a supplier who cannot
   hold a tolerance should say so at quote time, not after the first production run.
2. Send the identical RFQ to every supplier on the shortlist, with the same requested volume tiers and the same
   response deadline.
3. Collect quotes across every requested tier. A supplier who only quotes one tier gets asked again before being
   compared.
4. Flag any quote missing a required certification or payment term; exclude it from the comparison until the gap
   is resolved.
5. Build the landed cost per unit for every quote at every tier (working with the landed cost calculator), and
   compare both unit cost and the cash impact of committing to a larger tier. Recommend one supplier and tier with
   the numbers shown, not just a lowest-price pick.

## Checks
- Every RFQ measurement matches the tech pack's own tolerance band.
- Every supplier quoted against the same terms and deadline.
- A flagged, incomplete quote never enters the final recommendation.

## Output
{rfq_document, quotes[{supplier, tier, price, terms}], flags[], recommendation}

## Example
RFQ sent to 4 verified suppliers for tiers 3,000 / 8,000 / 15,000 units. One quote flagged for missing a BIS
certificate. Recommendation: Supplier B at the 8,000 tier: lowest landed cost per unit among complete quotes, and
the cash impact fits the brand's stated cash cover.

# Run the 3-stage sample gate

## Purpose
No creative shoot, price commitment or launch date happens before a sample from the exact factory clears this gate
against an approved reference. Working from memory or a photo instead of a physical reference produces drift no one
notices until a full production run fails.

## Steps
1. Confirm the approved reference sample is physically in-house before starting any comparison. If it only exists
   at the factory, stop and get it shipped first.
2. Run the 3-stage comparison: pre-production sample against reference, production sample against reference, and a
   pulled sample from the actual shipped batch against reference. Compare side by side on every dimension the tech
   pack specifies.
3. Score the factory's communication and reliability during the round: response time to questions, accuracy of
   what they claimed versus what arrived: separate from the physical sample's quality.
4. Record pass, hold or reject for each stage, with the exact deviation stated as a measurement (e.g., "wall
   thickness 2.1mm vs. spec 3mm ± 0.2mm"), never as an impression.

## Checks
- No stage begins without a confirmed, physical in-house reference.
- Every stage has a recorded result, none skipped.
- Every deviation is a number against the tech pack, not a subjective note.

## Output
{stage_results[{stage, result, deviation}], reliability_score, overall}

## Example
Stage 1: pass. Stage 2: hold: zipper pull 4mm shorter than spec, reference confirmed 6mm minimum. Factory
responded to the flag within 24 hours with a corrected sample. Stage 2 re-run: pass. Overall: pass, logged with the
one recorded deviation and its resolution.

# Negotiate a cost-down with real leverage

## Purpose
Asking for a discount with no leverage rarely moves price and can damage the relationship. This skill builds real
leverage first, then negotiates from it, and never asks for a cost-down that would strain the relationship for more
than it is worth.

## Steps
1. Build real leverage before asking for anything: a vetted, willing alternate factory at a comparable or better
   price; a teardown of a competitor's comparable product showing where cost could come out; the category's normal
   factory margin so an ask is grounded in what is realistic, not arbitrary.
2. Present the ask with the specific leverage named plainly: "we have a comparable quote at X" carries far more
   weight than "can you do better."
3. Confirm the final price and terms in writing before treating the negotiation as closed.
4. Book the production slot at the exact factory that passed the sample gate: never a sister factory or a
   different production line, even if it is cheaper.

## Checks
- The leverage used is real: a vetted alternate that genuinely exists, not an empty threat.
- The booked slot is confirmed at the exact factory and line that passed the sample.

## Output
{leverage[], ask, outcome{price, terms}, slot_booked}

## Example
Leverage: a verified backup factory quoted 8% lower for the same spec. Ask presented with that quote referenced.
Outcome: factory matched within 3%, citing relationship history; final terms locked at 30/70 split. Slot booked for
week 6 at the same factory that passed the sample.

# Monitor supplier performance and commodity cost

## Purpose
A supplier vetted once at onboarding can still drift. This skill runs the standing, ongoing side of the
relationship: a real scorecard on delivery and quality, and a watch on the commodity inputs that quietly move a
SKU's cost even when the supplier's own price stays flat.

## Steps
1. Score every active supplier on a fixed set of measures: on-time delivery rate, defect rate, responsiveness to
   queries, and price stability over time. Use the supplier's actual order history, never an impression from the
   last conversation.
2. Track the priced-in commodity inputs behind each SKU (cotton, resin, steel, whatever the product depends on) on
   a set monthly cadence, comparing against public commodity price indices.
3. When a cost-down looks possible, weigh it against the relationship-risk cost: a supplier pushed too hard on
   price may cut corners elsewhere or deprioritize the brand's orders during a capacity crunch.
4. Flag the result for the founder where the recommendation is "hold off" rather than "push," since that is the
   less obvious call.

## Checks
- The scorecard is built from real order data, not opinion.
- A commodity flag names the specific input and the specific price move, with its date.
- Any recommendation states which risk it is weighing against which saving.

## Output
{scorecard{on_time, defect_rate, responsiveness, price_stability}, commodity_flags[], risk_recommendation}

## Example
Scorecard: on-time 94%, defect rate 1.2%, responsiveness 18-hour average, price stable 6 months. Commodity flag:
input resin up 9% this month per index. Recommendation: hold on renegotiating this supplier's price given their
strong on-time record; absorb the resin move for one cycle and recheck next month.

# Structure payment terms and cash impact

## Purpose
The payment route and split on a sourcing deal is a real cash decision, not paperwork. This skill picks the route
that matches the actual relationship risk and hands Finance the full cash picture at every deal close, never a
verbal estimate.

## Steps
1. Choose the payment route: wire transfer, letter of credit, platform trade assurance, or escrow: based on the
   supplier relationship's real history and risk, not a fixed default used for every deal.
2. Structure the split: advance percentage, balance on shipment or delivery, and any retention held back pending
   the sample or inspection result. Confirm the MOQ this split assumes.
3. Compute, in code, the float days (time cash is committed before goods or revenue arrive), the total cash locked
   up at any point in the cycle, and any financing cost if the route involves one (LC fees, trade-assurance
   charges).
4. Package the full numbers into a packet Finance can act on immediately, without needing to ask a follow-up
   question.

## Checks
- The route chosen matches the relationship's actual risk level, stated explicitly.

# Clear a shipment for departure

## Purpose
A shipment that leaves uninspected, on the wrong freight mode, or with a 3PL picked on price alone turns into a
launch-date or cash problem weeks later. This skill runs the pre-departure checklist as one gate.

## Steps

   percentage. A SKU with a clean history gets a tighter buffer; one with past issues gets a wider one and closer
   scrutiny.

   discard. No unit is left undecided.

   to hit, and the cash the brand has available to cover air freight's premium.

hybrid (60% sea to save cash, 40% air to hit the launch date). 3PL selected on a 97% on-time history despite a 4%

## Purpose
A defect complaint that only gets logged as "SKU X has issues" cannot be fixed at the source. This skill traces the

   real exposure rather than treating this as an isolated incident.
3. Run the corrective-action loop with the supplier: identify the root cause together, agree the specific fix, and
   set a verification method (a re-inspection, a sample from the next run) before closing the loop.

# Compute reorder point and channel replenishment

## Purpose
A reorder point sized from trailing sales alone misses two India-specific risks: festive demand spikes and
COD-market RTO reversing what looked like a sale. It also misses that Amazon FBA has its own IPI and storage limits
that can block a restock even when stock is genuinely needed.

## Steps
1. Pull real velocity and real lead time per SKU per channel. A subscription or bundle SKU uses its committed
   cadence (what customers actually signed up for), never trailing sales, since trailing sales lag a subscription's
   real demand.
2. Compute reorder point and safety stock in code, with an explicit adjustment for India-specific spike risk:
   festive-season demand surges and the reversal risk from COD RTO.
3. Compare current stock against the computed reorder point and flag any SKU already below it or projected to fall
   below it within the lead time window.
4. For Amazon SKUs, size the FBA replenishment shipment from a real inventory-cover target, treating a stockout as
   the failure mode to avoid above almost any other cost. Check the current IPI score and storage limits before
   finalizing the shipment size, since a low IPI score can cap how much can be sent in.

## Checks
- Velocity and lead time are real, current numbers, never a stale default.
- The spike-risk adjustment is shown explicitly, not folded silently into the number.
- An IPI or storage-limit flag is raised before it blocks a planned restock, not after.

## Output
{sku, reorder_point, safety_stock, current_stock, status, fba_cover, ipi_flag}

## Example
SKU-1042: velocity 40/day, lead time 18 days, festive-adjusted safety stock +35%. Reorder point 1,080 units;
current stock 950: status: reorder now. FBA cover target 45 days; IPI score 420 (above the 400 threshold): no
restock block.

## Purpose
Two structural risks share one owner because both are about catching a slow-moving problem before it becomes an
expensive one: too much dependence on one supplier or country, and stock quietly ageing past the point it can be

   monthly calendar date, since a duty change can move margin materially overnight.

# Sync multi-channel stock and plan peak-season capacity

## Purpose
A stock pool split across channels without buffers oversells the moment two channels sell the last unit at once.
And a peak season fails in whichever of stock, staffing or system capacity was not planned for, not necessarily
the one that got the most attention. This skill keeps the pool synced day to day and plans for the season as one
combined picture.

## Steps
1. Keep one stock pool synced across every channel: site, marketplaces, quick commerce, physical stores: with a
   stated buffer per channel that prevents any one channel from overselling against real available stock.
2. Set order-routing and split-shipment rules by channel and warehouse, so an order is fulfilled from the right
   location without a person deciding case by case.
3. Ahead of the festive season, project the safety stock the season will need using at least one prior festive
   cycle's data where it exists, not a flat percentage bump.
4. Check warehouse staffing and WMS/OMS system load against that projected peak volume, expressed as a percentage
   of capacity used, not a yes/no guess.
5. Combine stock, staffing and system-load readiness into one plan, since a plan that only covers stock misses the
   two failure modes that actually cause a bad festive season.

## Checks
- No channel is allowed to oversell against its stated buffer.
- The readiness plan explicitly covers stock, staffing and system load together, not stock alone.

{sync_status, routing_rules[], peak_projection, capacity_check, readiness_plan}

## Example
Buffers set: site 5%, marketplaces 8% (slower stock sync), quick commerce 15% (fastest depletion risk). Peak
projection: Diwali week needs 2.4x baseline safety stock based on last year's data. Staffing check: current
warehouse shift covers 78% of projected peak pick volume: flagged for an extra shift.

# Select 3PL/WMS and build warehouse and returns operations

## Purpose
Three related decisions belong to one fulfilment manager: which 3PL and WMS to run on, how the warehouse actually
operates day to day, and what happens to every unit that comes back. Keeping them together avoids a WMS chosen
without the warehouse rules it needs to support, or a returns rule invented case by case after go-live.

1. Run the RFP and SLA negotiation for a domestic fulfilment 3PL: separate from any import-side freight or factory
   3PL, since the requirements differ (last-mile speed and accuracy versus long-haul cost).
2. Test the 3PL's WMS integration before go-live: order sync, stock sync, and returns feed, all tested end to end.
3. Set slotting rules by SKU velocity (fast movers closest to pack stations) and the pick-pack-QC method and
   staffing level against real, not projected, order volume.

# Screen an Amazon opportunity and mine reviews/keywords

## Purpose
A candidate that cleared the general product screen (PROD-C01-C05) still needs Amazon-specific diligence: Amazon's
own price dynamics, keyword search behaviour, and review patterns work differently from the open web or DTC.

## Steps
1. Apply Amazon-specific elimination screens: a price floor below which margin cannot work after fees, the price
   spread across page-1 listings (a huge spread signals a confusing or commoditized category), keyword search
   variability, and how dominant one or two brands already are in the category.
2. Run a real fad filter against the candidate's Amazon search trend data: a single-month spike is not the same
   as sustained demand.
3. Read 1 to 3 star reviews on the closest competing listings for complaints this candidate's design could fix. Use
   the complaint as a design input, never copy the review's wording into any copy.
4. Confirm mid-rated, high-volume sellers exist in the category as a demand-and-gap signal: real search volume
   with real dissatisfaction is the strongest opportunity signal available.
5. Mine keywords from reverse-ASIN tools for the category, ranked by search volume where the tool provides it.

## Checks
- Every elimination screen states its specific reason.
- The fad filter is based on more than one data point over time.
- No review text is copied verbatim; only the underlying gap it points to is used.

## Output
{screen_result, fad_verdict, complaint_list[], keyword_list[]}

## Example
Screen: pass (price floor clears with FBA fees included, page-1 spread moderate). Fad filter: pass, 3-year steady
growth not a single spike. Complaints mined: "lid doesn't seal after 2 months" appears in 40+ reviews across 3
competitors: a fixable design input. Keywords ranked by volume for the listing build.

# Model Amazon channel economics

## Purpose
Amazon's referral fee, FBA fee and storage cost stack up in ways that are easy to underestimate from memory. This
skill models the full stack in code against a SKU's real landed cost, so a launch or continuation decision is made
on a real net margin, not a gross-margin illusion.

## Steps
1. Pull the current, dated Amazon fee stack for the category: referral fee percentage, FBA pick-pack-ship fee by
   size tier, and storage cost by month.
2. Model the full fee stack against the SKU's landed cost, computed in code, never estimated.
3. Add a stated PPC budget assumption (clearly labeled as an assumption) and the storage cost for the SKU's actual
   size tier.
4. Check the resulting Amazon price against the brand's DTC price-parity rule, using the current live DTC price,
   not a stale one.
5. Compute net margin after every fee line, in code, and flag any SKU whose net margin falls below the brand's own
   stated floor.

## Checks
- Every fee line is sourced from Amazon's currently published rate card, dated.
- Net margin is computed in code, never estimated in prose.
- Price parity is checked against the live DTC price at the time of the check.

## Output
{fee_stack, net_margin_per_sku[], parity_check, margin_floor_flags[]}

## Example
SKU-1042: referral fee 15%, FBA fee ₹85 (size tier standard), storage ₹12/unit/month. Landed cost ₹210, Amazon
price ₹599. Net margin after all fees and a ₹40 PPC assumption: 19%, above the brand's 15% floor. Parity check:
Amazon price matches DTC within the allowed band.

# Prepare an FBA inbound shipment

## Purpose
FBA's dimension and weight limits change, and an outdated cached limit produces a rejected or delayed shipment.
Keeping the full paper trail matters because it is the only evidence available if inventory goes missing in
Amazon's own warehouse.

## Steps
1. Measure the actual case dimensions and check them against FBA's currently published hard limits, pulled fresh
   rather than from a cached figure from a past shipment.
2. Reuse a saved shipment template whenever this SKU and case size match a shipment already sent successfully,
   to avoid re-deriving the plan from scratch each time.
3. Build the shipment plan: box count, weight per box (checked under the carrier's per-box limit), and carrier
   choice.
4. Generate and check carton labels against FBA's current label specification before printing.
5. Keep the full paper trail: bill of lading, carrier receipt, carton count: so a later lost-inventory claim has
   the evidence it needs.
6. Confirm the shipment against Amazon's inbound dashboard once it is marked received, and flag any discrepancy
   between what was sent and what was received.

## Checks
- The dimension limits used are the currently published ones, not a cached figure.
- The paper trail is complete before the shipment physically leaves.

## Output
{dimension_check, shipment_plan, carton_labels, paper_trail, receipt_confirmation}

## Example
Case dimensions checked against FBA's current oversize threshold: under by 2cm. Template reused from the last
shipment of the same SKU. 40 cartons, weight checked under the carrier's 25kg/box limit. Paper trail filed; receipt
confirmed 6 days later with a 2-unit discrepancy flagged for a claim.

# Sequence an Amazon account, Brand Registry and launch

## Purpose
Account setup, trademark filing, Brand Registry enrolment and launch-week execution have a strict order: doing
them out of order (enrolling Brand Registry before the trademark is filed, for instance) causes rejections and
weeks of delay. This skill enforces the correct sequence.

## Steps
1. Get the Amazon seller account, business entity, payout details and identity verification right the first time
: a rejected or later-flagged account costs far more time than a careful first submission.
2. Sequence trademark filing before listing creation; Brand Registry cannot be enrolled without a filed trademark,
   so this step must complete first.
3. Once the trademark is filed and the listing (built via PROD-W22) is live, enrol Brand Registry.
4. Turn on the Storefront and Subscribe & Save benefits Brand Registry unlocks, confirming both are actually live,
   not just eligible.
5. Concentrate real demand into the first launch weeks by aligning stock arrival and PPC campaign start to the same
   date, and build a pre-launch audience where the platform's rules allow it.
6. Protect a novel product against copycats from day one: watermark product images, and file for design protection
   where the product is genuinely novel.

## Checks
- No step in the sequence is attempted before its prerequisite is confirmed complete.
- Stock and PPC go live on the same date, never staggered by more than a day.

## Output
{account_status, trademark_status, brand_registry_status, launch_plan, protection_checklist}

## Example
Account verified on first submission (2 weeks). Trademark filed before listing creation. Listing built and live.
Brand Registry enrolled once both prerequisites confirmed. Launch week: stock arrived and PPC campaign started the
same day; a pre-launch waitlist built the prior 2 weeks.

# Monitor marketplace health: reviews, account health, Buy Box

## Purpose
A policy notice ignored for a week can become a suspension; an unauthorized reseller undercutting on price can
erode a brand's own margin and trust. This skill runs the standing weekly health check that keeps both from
becoming a surprise.

## Steps
1. Request product reviews only through the platform's own permitted request mechanism: never an incentivised or
   off-platform review ask, which risks policy action against the account.
2. Contest any feedback that is misplaced (attached to the wrong product) or violates the platform's own feedback
   policy, through the platform's formal dispute process.
3. Check the Account Health dashboard every single week without exception, so a new policy notice is caught the
   week it appears, not discovered a month later as a suspension.
4. Check who holds the Buy Box across every marketplace listing, and check unauthorised reseller pricing against
   the brand's own MAP (minimum advertised price) policy.
5. Flag any MAP or price-integrity problem to the founder for a decision, rather than changing the brand's own
   price unilaterally in response.

## Checks
- Every review request uses a platform-permitted method.
- No price is changed by this agent in response to a MAP issue; it is always flagged to the founder.

## Output
{review_requests[], account_health_status, buy_box_report, map_violation_flags[]}

## Example
Account Health: clear, no new notices this week. Buy Box: held on 8 of 9 active listings; the 9th lost to an
unauthorized reseller pricing 12% below the brand's MAP: flagged for the founder rather than matching the price.

# Diagnose Amazon performance and plan growth

## Purpose
A sales drop on Amazon has at least two very different causes: fewer people seeing the listing, or fewer people
buying once they see it: and confusing the two leads to the wrong fix. This skill forces that split before any
other conclusion, and keeps growth responses inside Amazon's own compliant tools.

## Steps
1. Split any sales change into a traffic component and a conversion component, using Business Reports data, before
   drawing any conclusion about the product.
2. Check attribution (is the traffic even coming from where it looks like) and seasonality (is this the normal
   pattern for this time of year) before calling a product a failure based on a raw sales number.
3. Respond only with Amazon's own compliant promotion tools: Lightning Deals, Coupons, Amazon-native ad formats: 
   never an outside workaround that risks a policy violation.
4. Decide whether to add a second SKU based on the diagnosis, not on a hunch, and test smaller situational growth
   levers (FBM to FBA conversion, Small and Light enrolment, a design-vendor bake-off, Amazon Live) each with a
   defined read set before the test starts.
5. Write the one-page memo behind any decision to add or expand the Amazon channel.

## Checks
- The traffic/conversion split happens before any conclusion about the product itself.
- Every growth-lever test has its read defined before the test starts, never decided after seeing results.

## Output
{diagnosis{traffic_change, conversion_change}, promotion_response, growth_tests[], channel_memo}

## Example
Sales down 22% week over week. Diagnosis: traffic down 3% (normal seasonality), conversion down 19%: points to a
listing or price issue, not a demand problem. Response: a compliant Coupon test with a defined 2-week read, not an
off-platform discount code.

# Build, validate and audit the catalogue feed

## Purpose
Media buyer and Organic both depend on one clean feed to plug into shopping ads and marketplace channels, and a
broken image or a duplicate SKU discovered by a channel's own rejection wastes a cycle that a standing audit would
have caught first.

## Steps
1. Keep one clean master product feed: titles, images, prices, availability, and GTIN, with no duplicate SKU and
   no missing GTIN.
2. Validate the feed against each destination channel's own current schema before handing it off: a schema that
   worked last month may have changed.
3. Hand the validated feed to Media buyer and Organic, and confirm it loaded without error on their side.
4. Run a standing audit across every channel's live listings for broken images, missing attributes, and duplicate
   SKUs that may have crept in independently of the feed.
5. Check for the brand's own price mismatch between its site and each marketplace, flagging any gap rather than
   silently reconciling it.
6. Check every new product image and video against each channel's own size, crop and content rule before it is
   pushed, since a Blinkit thumbnail and an Amazon main image have entirely different requirements.

## Checks
- The feed has zero duplicate SKUs and zero missing GTINs before handoff.
- A price mismatch is always flagged, never quietly auto-corrected.
- Image and video specs are checked before push, not discovered via a channel's rejection.

## Output
{master_feed, validation_report, quality_audit_report, price_mismatch_report, asset_spec_flags[]}

## Example
Feed validated clean against Amazon's, Flipkart's and Blinkit's current schemas. Weekly audit found 3 SKUs with a
broken image link on one marketplace and a ₹20 price mismatch between site and Flipkart: both flagged, neither
auto-corrected.

# Onboard a brand on quick commerce

## Purpose
Quick commerce onboarding requires a specific document set and each platform runs its own review process and its
own unit-economics validation window (commonly around 90 days) before the brand is judged to be worth investing
in further. Missing a required document is the most common cause of onboarding delay.

## Steps
1. Assemble the GST, FSSAI, barcode and packaging documents the platform's own onboarding checklist requires,
   confirming every item is present before submission.
2. Submit through the platform's own onboarding channel, never a workaround or a third-party shortcut.
3. Track the document review status and respond to any query the platform raises within its stated window.
4. Prepare the initial catalogue listing using the matching Blinkit or Zepto listing skill.
5. Confirm the platform's own unit-economics validation window and what it requires the brand to demonstrate
   during it.
6. Get the brand live and confirm the first order flows correctly end to end before calling onboarding complete.

## Checks
- Every document the platform's checklist requires is present before submission.
- The validation window and its specific requirement are both logged, not assumed.

## Output
{document_packet, review_status, initial_listing, validation_window, go_live_confirmation}

## Example
Documents assembled: GST, FSSAI licence, barcode registration, packaging compliance declaration. Submitted through
the platform's seller onboarding portal. One query on FSSAI scope resolved within 2 days. First order confirmed to
flow correctly on day 12 of a stated 90-day validation window.

# Manage quick commerce ad credits and dark-store fill rate

## Purpose
Quick commerce platforms typically report ROAS on MRP, which overstates real return by 30 to 50 percent; judging
ad spend on that number leads to bad decisions. And a dark-store stockout triggers an algorithmic ranking penalty
that takes real time to recover from, so it needs daily, not weekly, attention.

## Steps
1. Spend each platform's ad tools deliberately rather than leaving credits unused, and pull back spend for a SKU
   once its organic search ranking improves and stops needing paid support.
2. Recompute ROAS from actual transaction value, never the platform's own MRP-based default, before judging
   whether spend is working.
3. Negotiate festive promotional windows ahead of the calendar date, since terms secured early are typically better
   than what is available once the festive rush begins.
4. Watch stock levels across the dark-store network daily, the way a merchandiser walks the shelf, and flag a
   stockout before it triggers the platform's own algorithmic ranking penalty, which is slow to recover from once
   triggered.

## Checks
- Every ROAS figure used for a decision is recomputed from transaction value, never quoted from the platform's
  MRP-based dashboard number.
- A fill-rate flag is raised before the ranking-penalty window closes, not after the penalty has already applied.

## Output
{ad_spend_plan, roas_recomputed, promo_terms, dark_store_report, stockout_flags[]}

## Example
Platform-reported ROAS: 4.2x (MRP-based). Recomputed from transaction value: 2.9x: spend plan adjusted down for
the weakest SKU. Dark-store report: 2 of 40 stores below reorder threshold, flagged same day, ahead of the
platform's ranking-penalty window.

# Track Legal Metrology, FSSAI and EPR compliance

## Purpose
Legal Metrology registration, FSSAI licensing and EPR plastic-packaging filing are each recurring, concrete
obligations that a brand either tracks deliberately or handles ad hoc under deadline pressure. This skill keeps
one register instead of three separate ones scattered across people's memory.

## Steps
1. Keep one register listing which SKUs require Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) registration or an FSSAI
   licence, based on their actual category.
2. Track each licence's current validity window, so an expiry is known well ahead of the date, not discovered
   after it lapses.
3. Flag the relabelling a SKU needs on any MRP or GST change: this is a common, easy-to-miss trigger distinct from
   a licence renewal.
4. Register the brand's plastic packaging under India's EPR rules, and track the annual filing deadline and
   recycling-target obligation.
5. Flag when a shortfall against the recycling target means the brand needs to buy EPR credits, stating the
   shortfall amount specifically.

## Checks
- Every licence's validity window reflects a checked, current status, never an assumption that it is still valid.
- A relabelling flag fires on every MRP or GST change, not only when a licence comes up for renewal.

## Output
{licence_register[], relabelling_flags[], epr_status, epr_shortfall_flag}

## Example
Licence register: 14 of 18 SKUs require Legal Metrology registration, all current. One FSSAI licence expiring in
45 days, flagged to the founder. A recent MRP change on 3 SKUs triggered a relabelling flag. EPR filing on track;
no shortfall this cycle.
